about: References written inside prose. In a knowledge base most of the graph lives in the writing rather than in the schema, and a format that only models declared reference fields cannot see it. The rule is that prose stays opaque and its edges are mirrored into relations, so a consumer that cannot read your dialect can still hold your graph — and knows what it is about to break.

cases.why: A tool with no prose at all still has to come out of this holding the edge. Mirroring inline references into relations is what makes that possible: the link between two notes is a fact about the library, and locking it inside one producer's markup dialect makes it a fact only that producer can read.

cases.why: Nobody has to understand double brackets, double parens, or whatever the next tool invents. The format deliberately does not standardize a markup dialect — it standardizes that yours comes back exactly as you wrote it. A consumer that normalizes prose into its own syntax has rewritten the user's writing, which is the one thing in a knowledge base nobody wants touched.

This is what the mirror buys. A tool that rewrites prose into its own markup cannot know whether it just destroyed a link, because it cannot parse the dialect it is replacing — but the relations array told it there was one. Without the mirror the loss is not merely unreported, it is undetectable.

A tool with only untyped backlinks must keep the type, and must keep where the edge came from. Flattening an inline mention and a declared reference field into the same undifferentiated link loses the difference between what someone wrote in a sentence and what they filled into a form, and only one of those can be edited without touching the prose.

The mirror is only trustworthy if it points at something real. An edge claiming to come from a field the type does not have is either a stale export or a producer guessing, and a consumer has no way to tell which — so it is caught here rather than becoming a link nobody can trace back to a sentence.

A link says one thing: this points at that. An edge with no far end is not a link with a piece missing, it is a row. Whatever a producer knows about the thing that isn't there — its name, what it ought to become — is knowledge about that thing, and belongs to an object rather than to the edge, where it would be a second copy of a fact drifting from the first.

Writing a name before the thing exists is normal, and the answer is not a broken link — it is a real object with a real id that has a name and no type yet. The link is ordinary. Everything unusual about the situation is on the object, where a consumer will look for it anyway, and where it can be corrected once rather than in every sentence.

An interface with one key for people and another for anything knows, at the moment of writing, which was reached for. That is real information and nothing else records it, so it is worth keeping — as a suggestion about the stub, not as a claim on the link. It is what lets a tool offer to create a person rather than an untyped stub, and it is only ever a suggestion: whatever the thing turns out to be, the thing is authoritative.

The same object as the case above, once somebody said what it was: the stub flag is gone, a type is on, and the id never moved — so every link pointing at it is still correct and nothing had to be rewritten. This is the whole reason to mint an id at the moment of writing. A producer that instead keeps the name inside the prose has to find and edit every piece of writing that mentioned it, atomically, and tell every open editor to reread.

A type id is one producer's private key. Saying a stub should become `t_person_4a91` tells a stranger nothing, and tells the same producer nothing once that type is deleted. The format already has a vocabulary for what something is, and a suggestion the receiving tool cannot read is not a suggestion, it is a note to self.
